newsitem.title: USA: Former Mexican official took drug bribes - jury.
newsitem.headline: Former Mexican official took drug bribes - jury.

text.p: A U.S. jury on Saturday ruled in a civil trial that former Mexican deputy attorney general Mario Ruiz Massieu took millions of dollars in bribes from drug-traffickers and stashed the money in a Texas bank.

But the jury, after day-long deliberations, also said that Ruiz Massieu had not laundered the money and let him keep $1.1 million of a $9 million bank account seized two years ago by the U.S. government.
Ruiz Massieu was attempting in the trial to get all of the money back, but the jury's decision meant the U.S. government, pending appeal, will keep $7.9 million
Ruiz Massieu showed little emotion when the decision was read, but his wife, Eugenia Barrientos, said he was "pleased."
"That we won something is better than losing everything," she told reporters.
The split decision was the result of the eight-member jury having to answer four questions about the source of the money.

On three, which had to do with whether the money had come from drugs, the jury said yes. But on a fourth, about whether he had attempted to launder the money, they said no, which apparently led to the decision to let him keep part of the $9 million.
Prosecutors said Ruiz Massieu took bribes from Mexican drug lords in exchange for protection while he was in the Mexican Attorney General's office and supposedly a top drug-fighter in 1993 and 1994.

Witnesses included former police bodyguard Raul Macias, who said he put two suitcases full of drug cash in Ruiz Massieu's car in an August 1994 rendezvous outside the Attorney General's headquarters in downtown Mexico City.

Ruiz Massieu testified the $9 million was part of his family's fortune, stashed in the United States for safekeeping from instability in Mexico. He said the fortune came partly from lavish government bonuses paid to high-ranking officials out of a secret budget controlled by the President of Mexico.

Ruiz Massieu said the United States took his money because the Mexican government was angered at his charges that the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) obstructed his investigation into his brother's assassination.

Brother Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu, then the PRI's general secretary, was gunned down in Mexico City in September 1994. Mexican officials said Mario Ruiz Massieu covered up the alleged involvement of Raul Salinas de Gortari, the jailed brother of former President Carlos Salinas de Gortari, in the killing.

Before the trial began, news reports citing court documents said prosecutors had informants who would link the Ruiz Massieu brothers to a conspiracy run by members of the Salinas family, not including the former president, to protect drug-traffickers in exchange for money.

The Salinas family denied the allegations, but defence attorney Tony Canales asked for permission to question Raul Salinas, who has been jailed for two years in Mexico on charges he masterminded the murder of Jose Francisco Ruiz Massieu.
The request was approved by U.S. District Judge Nancy Atlas, but the deposition apparently never took place because neither Salinas nor several other potentially explosive witnesses appeared.

Still, U.S. prosecutors were not shy about charging during the trial that drug corruption in Mexico, particularly among law enforcement officials, was rampant. "The Mexican federal judicial police, people in the PGR (Mexican Attorney General's office), deputy attorney generals or that level at least, are involved, or have been involved (in drug-trafficking)," prosecutor Jesse Rodriguez said in closing arguments on Friday.

One government witness, a now-jailed member of the Gulf drug cartel in northern Mexico, testified that the cartel paid bribes "all the way to the top in Mexico City," while another, a former Mexican police officer, said government planes were used to ferry drug bribes to officials in the Mexican capital.

Ruiz Massieu will return to New Jersey where he is under house arrest awaiting an upcoming deportation hearing that could force him to return to Mexico to face charges. He applied for political asylum in the United States on grounds that his life would be in danger in Mexico, said defence attorney Tony Canales.
